newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan's MITI draws roadmap for structural reform.
newsitem.headline: Japan's MITI draws roadmap for structural reform.

text.p: Japan on Monday unveiled a roadmap for structural reforms to its economy to help make the nation's industries more cost-competitive within five years.

The report comes after Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto instructed the Ministry of International Trade and Industry (MITI) in mid-November to compile a reform plan in light of the rapid ageing of Japan's population and a sluggish job market.

"I believe the plan is a broad and comprehensive one which goes one step further than past deregulation efforts," MITI Vice Minister Tsutomu Makino told a news conference on Monday when presenting the report.
It was compiled by MITI after consulting with other ministries, Makino said, and will help implement some of the reforms Hashimoto promised in a re-election speech in mid-November.
The report, which does not cover the "Big Bang" financial industry reforms which Hashimoto has also called for, is expected to be approved at a cabinet meeting on Tuesday.

"If approved by the cabinet, this (plan) becomes a government promise, the strongest commitment possible on the part of the administration," Makino said after reporters questioned whether the government would carry out the broad deregulation measures.

The report calls for building an infrastructure necessary to nurture new businesses in industries expected to expand in the near future. It also aims to expand Japan's job market, now suffering as an increasing number of businesses move from Japan to countries where they can operate more cheaply.
The report lists 15 industries, including communications, medicine, energy, housing and biotechnology, as targets for deregulation.

It also offers some 500 concrete recommendations for reform, and the government plans to submit 15 bills related to the reforms at the next ordinary session of parliament, which convenes in January, Makino said.
The government is expected to propose additional measures, including how to implement the recommendations and a timetable, by the spring.
